newsitem.title: THAILAND: Confusion hits Thai deposit protection scheme.
newsitem.headline: Confusion hits Thai deposit protection scheme.

text.p: Thousands of investors holding promissory notes with 16 suspended Thai finance firms faced confusion on Monday as they tried to withdraw their money following a government-imposed industry shakeup.

The 16 firms are being forced to merge with healthier ones in a scheme announced on Friday aimed at bolstering the finance sector, an area which has been hit hard by overexposure to the country's depressed property market.
But on Monday, confusion surrounded the plan, depositors amd company officials said.

Local authorities had promised after the firms were suspended on Friday that depositors should not worry about their money because they could exchange their paper at five leading government-nominated firms.

Depositors facing cash flow problems as a result of the suspensions were also told that they could take loans to tide them over from state-backed Krungthai Thanakit Plc at a discount to the face value of the notes.
But thousands of frustrated local depositors of the suspended firms called in to transfer their money only to find that it was not available on demand.

"The firm told me that it cannot do anything at the moment and we have to wait for 30 days before we can withdraw the money. I don't recall hearing that from the authorities," said a depositor with more than 20 million baht ($806,000) in a troubled firm.

Others who lined the lobbies of suspended finance firms on Monday said they were facing problems receiving extra documentation required to apply for the note scheme. They said the firms had still not received notification from the central bank allowing them to issue supporting documentation.

"I don't understand the whole procedure," said note-holder Nipa Visansawat, 73, who said that suspended G.C.N. Finance Plc, had told her the same story. Note holders also faced similar difficulties at other suspended firms.
Foreign and corporate creditors of suspended firms also found themselves in a lurch.

"We are still in the dark. So far only a depositor protection plan has been spelled out. But nothing concrete on the fate of creditors, including holders of debentures of the doomed companies, has been said," said a Hong Kong-based fund manager.
But KTT executives blamed suspended firms for not cooperating fully to make the depositor scheme a success.
Under the scheme, note holders of the 16 firms had to contact the issuing firm first if they wanted to get loans from KTT, they added.

"The finance company will forward all the necessary documents of customers seeking loans to us (Krungthai Thanakit). It will take us only a few days before we can give loans to promissory note holders," Phirasilp Subhapholsiri, president of Krungthai Thanakit, told reporters.

But the repayment period on Krungthai Thanakit loans is very short. Loan seekers must pay back the loan plus an average minimum overdraft rate charged by all domestic commercial banks plus a 1.5 percent service fee by July 31.

"Promissory note holders of those 16 finance firms can get loans from our company. Local commercial banks have promised that they would support this scheme and would loan us the money during the 30 days period," said Phirasilp.

Krungthai Thanakit officials said if the value of promissory notes was less than one million baht ($40,000), the borrowing limit was 60 percent of the total value and for other amounts on a sliding scale.
"The lending scheme is designed to help promissory note holders who need cash now. I still don't know how big the demand is at present," Phirasilp said.
Arporn Chewakrengkai, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfrell, said the central bank should set up a hot line to answer all questions the public might have and clear confusion.
"Confusion is expected at the start. If the government does not want the public to be panicked, they must give them access to right information," she said. ($ = 24.8 baht)
